references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew tells the same story: "And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions" ([ref:Matt 22:46|Matthew 22:46]). Jesus had answered all the challenging questions so convincingly that his opponents no longer dared to confront him.

Mark's parallel account states that "no one dared to ask him any more questions" ([ref:Mark 12:34|Mark 12:34]). In Mark's version, this is linked to Jesus commending the scribe who answered wisely about the greatest commandment.

Earlier in the Gospel of Luke, we find a similar situation where Jesus' opponents were unable to answer him: "They could not answer him" ([ref:Luk 14:6|Luke 14:6]), when Jesus challenged the Pharisees regarding healing on the Sabbath.

Earlier in the same chapter, after the question about paying taxes to Caesar, it is reported that his opponents "could not trap him in what he said before the people, and they marveled at his answer and were silenced" ([ref:Luk 20:26|Luke 20:26]). This shows an escalating silence among Jesus' opponents throughout the chapter.

The scribes and chief priests wanted to seize Jesus, but they feared the people ([ref:Luk 20:19|Luke 20:19]). Throughout the entire chapter, Jesus' opponents try to trap him with questions, but he overcomes them again and again, culminating in their no longer daring to ask anything.

Job's friends were also brought to silence: "They were afraid; they did not answer any more; they had no words" ([ref:Job 32:15-16|Job 32:15-16]). Silence as a response to overwhelming wisdom is a recurring biblical theme.
